  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A2" title="In Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B </span>Analysis</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_appendix">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A2.SS1" title="In Appendix B Analysis ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B.1 </span>Memory-Computation Trade-off Decoding</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A2.SS2" title="In Appendix B Analysis ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B.2 </span>Towards Memory: Compared to T-MAC</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A2.SS3" title="In Appendix B Analysis ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B.3 </span>Towards Compute: Compared to TQ1_0</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A3" title="In Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">C </span>Potential</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_appendix">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A3.SS1" title="In Appendix C Potential ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">C.1 </span>Bandwidth</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A3.SS2" title="In Appendix C Potential ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">C.2 </span>Instructions Throughput</span></a></li>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The advent of 1-bit large language models (LLMs), led by BitNet b1.58, has spurred interest in ternary LLMs. Despite this, research and practical applications focusing on efficient edge inference for ternary LLMs remain scarce. To bridge this gap, we introduce Bitnet.cpp, an inference system optimized for BitNet b1.58 and ternary LLMs. Given that <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">mixed-precision matrix multiplication (mpGEMM)</span> constitutes the bulk of inference time in ternary LLMs, Bitnet.cpp incorporates a novel mpGEMM library to facilitate sub-2-bits-per-weight, efficient and lossless inference. The library features two core solutions: <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ternary Lookup Table (TL)</span>, which addresses spatial inefficiencies of previous bit-wise methods, and <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Int2 with a Scale (I2_S)</span>, which ensures lossless edge inference, both enabling high-speed inference. Our experiments show that Bitnet.cpp achieves up to a 6.25x increase in speed over full-precision baselines and up to 2.32x over low-bit baselines, setting new benchmarks in the field. Additionally, we expand TL to element-wise lookup table (ELUT) for low-bit LLMs in the appendix, presenting both theoretical and empirical evidence of its considerable potential. Bitnet.cpp is publicly available at <a href="https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet/tree/paper" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet/tree/paper</a>, offering a sophisticated solution for the efficient and practical deployment of edge LLMs.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In recent years, large language models have garnered widespread attention due to their exceptional performance across a variety of tasks. However, the growing demand for efficient deployment on edge devices, particularly driven by data privacy concerns, poses challenges due to the limited computational power and bandwidth of these devices.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/title.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/358;" width="476" height="358"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>A comparison of end-to-end inference speeds on a 100B ternary LLM. <math id="S1.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(bx)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(bx)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the bits per weight, where <math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> denotes specific value. "N/A" indicates that the tested CPU cannot host the specified model size with the given kernel.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/lossless.svg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/106;" width="476" height="106"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>An example to demonstrate lossless inference for BitNet b1.58 with Bitnet.cpp.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, model compression techniques are frequently employed. Notable examples benefiting from such techniques include Gemini-Nano <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2024)</a></cite> and Phi3-mini <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdin et al. (2024)</a></cite>, both designed for mobile and personal devices. Furthermore, recent advancements by BitNet b1.58 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2024)</a></cite> represent a significant development in edge LLM inference, introducing 1-bit LLMs by quantizing all weights to ternary values therefore reducing the bits per weight (bpw) to 1.58, while preserving accuracy comparable to full-precision LLMs. Subsequent releases of ternary LLMs, including TriLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaushal et al. (2024)</a></cite>, Llama3-8B-1.58 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mekkouri et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and BitNet a4.8 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024a)</a></cite>, have demonstrated the effectiveness and applicability of ternary architectures, thereby extending the boundaries of the 1-bit era. Despite the burgeoning interest in ternary LLMs, the conversion of their theoretical benefits into practical advantages during inference is still understudied.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To fill this gap, we aim to enhance the performance of ternary LLMs edge inference by optimizing mpGEMM (e.g., 8-bit activation and 1.58-bit weight). However, the non-integer bpw characteristic of ternary weights conflicts with the rules for computer memory access alignment, thus posing challenges in designing a sub-2-bit-per-weight, efficient edge mpGEMM for ternary LLMs. Currently, TQ1_0 in llama.cpp<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">lla ()</a></cite> utilizes 1.69 bits to store ternary weights, but it is slower compared to TQ2_0 and T-MAC<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2024)</a></cite>, which use 2 bits to maintain alignment. Moreover, prior implementations of mpGEMM have not achieved lossless inference for BitNet b1.58, as they fail to fully align with BitNet b1.58 training schemes during inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address these issues, we develop Bitnet.cpp, which incorporates a novel mpGEMM library. Our key idea is to avoid intricate bit-level manipulations by directly operating the weight elements when designing mpGEMM, while strictly aligning with BitNet b1.58 training schemes. Based on our ideas, the library not only resolves spatial inefficiencies, but also surpasses existing solutions in terms of performance (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), achieving lossless inference for BitNet b1.58 (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). To this end, our work makes several contributions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">First, we conduct a comprehensive survey of current cutting-edge mpGEMM methods and identify their limitations when applied to ternary LLMs. (Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Ternary LLM &amp; mpGEMM on Edge ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To overcome these limitations, we design and implement a ternary mpGEMM library incorporating our innovative kernels, <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TL</span> and <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">I2_S</span>, which we integrate into Bitnet.cpp. This library facilitates fast and lossless inference through element-wise design and precise alignment with training schemes. (Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate Bitnet.cpp on multiple edge devices and demonstrate that it achieves a up to 6.25x speedup compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while realizing lossless inference for BitNet b1.58. (Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, in the appendix, we extend TL beyond ternary LLMs, to element-wise lookup table (ELUT) for low-bit LLMs. We perform both theoretical (Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Insight ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>) and practical (Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Analysis ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>) analyses of ELUT, demonstrating its high efficiency and untapped potential. (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Potential ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Ternary LLM &amp; mpGEMM on Edge</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present a detailed examination of the characteristics of ternary LLMs and introduce a systematic taxonomy of current edge mpGEMM methods, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Ternary LLM: Features ‣ 2 Ternary LLM &amp; mpGEMM on Edge ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. We aim to delineate the limitations of existing mpGEMM approaches in handling ternary LLMs, informed by our comprehensive survey, with the objective of guiding future optimizations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Ternary LLM: Features</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ternary Weights</span>
A distinctive characteristic of ternary LLMs is that the weights in the transformer layers are ternary, allowing only three possible values: {-1, 0, 1}. Consequently, the information content of these weights is approximately 1.58 bits per weight, as calculated by <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log(3)/\log(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log(3)/\log(2)</annotation></semantics></math>. This substantial compression not only markedly reduces the model size, but also enables opportunities for further optimization with existing mpGEMM methods, such as those employed in llama.cpp and T-MAC.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lossless Inference for BitNet b1.58</span>
BitNet b1.58 performs ternary quantization on weights and int8 per-tensor quantization on activations during training. Based on this, if the training constraints are preserved during inference, lossless inference can be achieved for BitNet b1.58, as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/classification.svg" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/289;" width="476" height="289"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>A taxonomy of mpGEMM solutions for ternary LLMs on edge devices. TL and I2_S are integrated in Bitnet.cpp, while QX and TQX are integrated in llama.cpp.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>mpGEMM on Edge: Definitions</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MAD-based and LUT-based</span>
We classify edge mpGEMM methods into two computational strategies: <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">multiply-then-add (MAD)-based</span> and <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">lookup table (LUT)-based</span>. The MAD-based strategy performs dot product calculations, while the LUT-based strategy employs lookup tables to store precomputed values, thereby enabling rapid accumulation via table lookups.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bit-wise and Element-wise</span>
Edge mpGEMM methods are additionally classified based on the fundamental unit of computation into <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bit-wise</span> and <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Element-wise</span> categories. Bit-wise methods process data at the bit level, focusing solely on bit operation without considering the attributes of weight elements, precluding non-integer bits per weight. In contrast, element-wise methods perform computations at the element level, taking into account the distinct properties of each weight element, which enables non-integer bits per weight.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>mpGEMM on Edge: Taxonomy (Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Ternary LLM: Features ‣ 2 Ternary LLM &amp; mpGEMM on Edge ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>)</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bit-wise LUT-based (Up left)</span>
Recent research by T-MAC has shown that bit-wise LUT-based methods significantly outperform MAD-based approaches in edge inference, particularly emphasizing their efficiency for low-bit LLMs. However, when applied to ternary LLMs, these bit-wise LUT-based methods exhibit spatial inefficiencies, leading to a substantial performance decline in environments with limited bandwidth.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bit-wise MAD-based (Down left)</span>
As a foundational framework for LLM edge inference, llama.cpp has pioneered several low-bit edge mpGEMM methods, predominantly bit-wise MAD-based, including the QX_0 and QX_K series. For instance, Q2_K utilizes the K-quants method to quantize weights to 2 bits, thereby ensuring the universality and correctness of the quantization. However, the application of Q2_K to ternary weights introduces complications: in addition to wasted space, maintaining accuracy with K-quants necessitates a multi-step dequantization process prior to performing the dot product, consequently increasing the overall latency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Element-wise MAD-based (Down right)</span>
In fact, llama.cpp introduces two element-wise MAD-based methods for ternary LLMs: TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, with bits per weight of 1.69 and 2.06, respectively. These methods leverage the ternary nature of the weights to avoid the multi-step dequantization required by K-quants, thereby significantly boosting performance. Despite these advancements, the lack of support for tensor-wide quantization means llama.cpp relies on per-block quantization with a static block length of 256 for activations (e.g., Q8_K). To accommodate this limitation, TQX_0 also utilizes the block quantization scheme. However, this approach is inconsistent with the computational methods used during BitNet b1.58 training, thus hindering TQX_0 from achieving lossless inference.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/typenewnew.svg" id="S2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/119;" width="476" height="119"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>A simple example to explain the differences between various methods for completing mpGEMM when <math id="S2.F4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=4</annotation></semantics></math>: (1) represents the MAD-based solution, where the result is obtained via the dot product; (2) represents the bit-wise LUT-based solution, where the weights are split into different bit indices, and the result is obtained by performing a lookup in the LUT, followed by bit-shifting and accumulation; (3) represents the element-wise LUT-based solution, where all possible values of the weights are enumerated to obtain the index, and the result is obtained by performing a lookup in the LUT, followed by accumulation. <math id="S2.F4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> refers to the <math id="S2.F4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{th}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{th}</annotation></semantics></math> bit in weight <math id="S2.F4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>. In (2), <math id="S2.F4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=4</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.F4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b=2</annotation></semantics></math>; whereas in (3) <math id="S2.F4.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.F4.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=3</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section addresses the limitations of existing edge mpGEMM methods, as previously discussed, through the design and implementation of a novel ternary mpGEMM library, summarized in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. We aim to showcase our pioneering techniques for efficient edge inference of ternary LLMs, focusing on two key dimensions: fast and lossless.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Fast Edge Inference</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For MAD-based methods, llama.cpp has implemented TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, which facilitate rapid ternary LLM edge inference. However, the current bit-wise approach for LUT-based methods does not fully exploit the potential of ternary LLMs for fast edge inference. Consequently, we have developed the <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">element-wise LUT-based (ELUT) mpGEMM</span>, which not only reduces bpw but also addresses the spatial inefficiencies inherent in bit-wise methods through <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">element-wise mirror consolidation</span>. To effectively implement ELUT in ternary LLMs, noted as <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TL</span>, we mitigate issues such as misaligned memory access through <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">signed-unsigned weight splitting</span>, overcome hardware instruction support deficiencies with <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1bit sign operation</span>, and resolve misaligned block computations via <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">block-fitting weight splitting</span>. This subsection will elaborate on our design and implementation strategies. For an in-depth analysis of the reasons behind ELUT’s acceleration and its broader implications beyond ternary LLMs, please refer to Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Insight ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>Design: TL</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Element-wise LUT-based mpGEMM</span>
The bit-wise LUT-based mpGEMM, designed for generality, uses 2-bit storage for ternary weights, leading to space inefficiency, thus negatively affecting speed. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an element-wise LUT-based mpGEMM approach. In the following, we delineate the key distinctions among MAD-based, bit-wise LUT-based, and element-wise LUT-based mpGEMM methods.</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=\sum_{i\leftarrow 1}^{K}A_{i}W_{i}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=\sum_{i\leftarrow 1}^{K}A_{i}W_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=\sum_{i\leftarrow 1}^{b}\sum_{j\leftarrow 1}^{K/g}\text{Look-up}(bLUT_{j},W_{ij})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>b</mi></munderover><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></munderover><mrow><mtext>Look-up</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=\sum_{i\leftarrow 1}^{b}\sum_{j\leftarrow 1}^{K/g}\text{Look-up}(bLUT_{j},W_{ij})</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

</table>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Consider a simple GEMM computation involving two input matrices: <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> (1, K) and <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> (K, 1). As shown in Equation <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.1.1 Design: TL ‣ 3.1 Fast Edge Inference ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, MAD-based mpGEMM computes the result using the dot product. In LUT-based mpGEMM, the conventional approach employs a bit-wise representation of the LUT, as shown in Equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.1.1 Design: TL ‣ 3.1 Fast Edge Inference ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the bit-width of the weight (2 for ternary weights, as <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3&lt;2^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3&lt;2^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>), and <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> represents the group size. The bit-wise LUT (<math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bLUT" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bLUT</annotation></semantics></math>) has a size of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^{g}</annotation></semantics></math>. By relaxing the bit-width restriction and adopting an element-wise representation of the LUT, as shown in Equation <a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3.1.1 Design: TL ‣ 3.1 Fast Edge Inference ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, a finer-grained expression is obtained. In this case, the element-wise LUT (<math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="eLUT" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">eLUT</annotation></semantics></math>) has a size of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{g}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the cardinality of the weight set (<math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> for ternary weights). Figure <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 2.3 mpGEMM on Edge: Taxonomy (Figure ) ‣ 2 Ternary LLM &amp; mpGEMM on Edge ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> illustrates a simple example highlighting these differences.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/tl2-design.svg" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/300;" width="476" height="300"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>The TL2 design uses signed-unsigned weight splitting. First, a 4-bit index weight is used to look up the table and obtain the unsigned result. Then, the corresponding 1-bit sign weight is applied to perform the sign operation on the unsigned result, yielding the final output.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Element-wise Mirror Consolidation</span>
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduced the concept of mirror consolidation, positing that during LUT enumeration, half of the values for <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^{g}</annotation></semantics></math> are inversely related to the other half, effectively halving the LUT size. Extending this concept to <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{g}</annotation></semantics></math> results in what we term element-wise mirror consolidation. For the element-wise LUT-based solution, due to the 128-bit SIMD register instruction length (e.g., AVX2 vpshufb), <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{g}</annotation></semantics></math> is constrained to a maximum of 16 (<math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times int8=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times int8=128</annotation></semantics></math>). Without element-wise mirror consolidation, the maximum value of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> for ternary LLMs remains at 2, maintaining the same bpw as the bit-wise LUT-based method (4 bits for 2 weights, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3^{2}&lt;2^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3^{2}&lt;2^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>). However, employing element-wise mirror consolidation increases the maximum <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> to 3, thus compressing bpw to 1.67 (5 bits for 3 weights, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{3^{3}}{2}&lt;2^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{3^{3}}{2}&lt;2^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>). Consequently, we have developed two practical designs for TL. We refer to the design with <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=2</annotation></semantics></math> as TL1 and the design with <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=3</annotation></semantics></math>, which incorporates element-wise mirror consolidation, as TL2. Algorithm <a href="#algorithm3" title="In Appendix D TL Algorithm ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> details the design of TL1, while Algorithm <a href="#algorithm4" title="In Appendix D TL Algorithm ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> outlines that of TL2.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>Implementation: TL</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Signed-Unsigned Weight Splitting</span>
To implement element-wise mirror consolidation, we introduce signed-unsigned weight splitting, where we use a separate 1-bit sign weight to store the sign of the enumeration, and a 4-bit index weight to store the corresponding LUT index for unsigned enumeration. It is evident that using continuous 5-bit storage for 3 weights would cause severe memory access misalignment. Since LUT-based mpGEMM is inherently memory-intensive, the additional memory accesses caused by misalignment would significantly degrade performance. In contrast, signed-unsigned weight splitting allows three weights to be represented using 5 bits, adhering to the element-wise approach, while simultaneously avoiding misalignment issues in computation and memory access. Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.1.1 Design: TL ‣ 3.1 Fast Edge Inference ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> demonstrates the detailed computation flow of TL2, using signed-unsigned weight splitting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1bit Sign Operation</span>
Determining the sign of the value indexed from the LUT using only 1 bit is challenging, as values are represented in two’s complement, and the design must ensure compatibility with SIMD instructions.</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E5X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E5X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle x=\text{sign}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>sign</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle x=\text{sign}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E5X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\oplus(\text{sign}+x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">⊕</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>sign</mtext><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\oplus(\text{sign}+x)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E5Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E5Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle x\in\text{int8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mtext>int8</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle x\in\text{int8}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E5Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle,\ \text{sign}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mtext>sign</mtext><mo>∈</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle,\ \text{sign}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">After evaluating multiple methods, we selected the approach presented in Equation <a href="#S3.E5" title="In 3.1.2 Implementation: TL ‣ 3.1 Fast Edge Inference ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> to address the issue. This sequence of operations, which includes the XOR and ADD operations, enables the sign to be determined by a single bit and is fully compatible with both the AVX2 and NEON instructions. When the bit of sign is 0, the result remains unchanged; otherwise, the result is converted to its negative value.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/padding.svg" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/171;" width="476" height="171"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>The computation sequences for TL1 and TL2. The left side represents TL1, and the right side represents TL2. Arrows indicate the order of computation, with the smallest computational unit being the compute block. <math id="S3.F6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.F6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> refer to the dimensions of the weights. <math id="S3.F6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bm\times by" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bm\times by</annotation></semantics></math> refers to the number of weights involved in the minimal compute block. <math id="S3.F6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bm</annotation></semantics></math> can be selected from 16 or 32. In TL1, <math id="S3.F6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="by" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">by</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S3.F6.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{256}{bm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>256</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{256}{bm}</annotation></semantics></math>, and in TL2, <math id="S3.F6.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="by" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">by</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S3.F6.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{192}{bm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>192</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{192}{bm}</annotation></semantics></math>.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Block-fitting Weight Splitting</span>
The TL series employs an LUT-centric data layout for mpGEMM to address inefficiencies in memory storage and access, as introduced by T-MAC. When adopting this layout, it is crucial to ensure that the minimal compute blocks align precisely with the weight matrix. As illustrated on the left side of Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3.1.2 Implementation: TL ‣ 3.1 Fast Edge Inference ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, for TL1, the block length <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="BK" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">BK</annotation></semantics></math> must be divisible by the matrix dimension <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>. This condition is easily met in TL1, as <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=2</annotation></semantics></math>, meaning <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> only needs to be a multiple of 2. However, the situation differs for TL2. Most LLM weight shapes do not have <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> as a multiple of 3 when using TL2, where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=3</annotation></semantics></math>. To address this, we introduce block-fitting weight splitting, which statically divides the weight into two parts to fit the blocks. After splitting, as shown on the right side of Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3.1.2 Implementation: TL ‣ 3.1 Fast Edge Inference ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, one portion of the weight, with dimensions <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ThreeK=\lfloor\frac{K}{BK3}\rfloor\times BK3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mfrac><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ThreeK=\lfloor\frac{K}{BK3}\rfloor\times BK3</annotation></semantics></math>, is computed using TL2, while the remaining portion, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="TwoK=K-ThreeK" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">TwoK=K-ThreeK</annotation></semantics></math>, is computed using TL1. By applying block-fitting weight splitting, we resolve the block mismatch issue without requiring additional padding, thereby preventing potential latency increases.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/f_compa.svg" id="S3.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/278;" width="476" height="278"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>End-to-end performance for inference on multiple model sizes, specific details of the model size are referenced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite>. Here, <math id="S3.F7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(bx)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(bx)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the bpw value, where <math id="S3.F7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> represents the respective bpw. Detailed performance information can be found on Table <a href="#A5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix E Performance ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Lossless Edge Inference</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To achieve lossless inference for BitNet b1.58, this subsection first identifies the gaps between existing methods and lossless inference. It then presents innovative approaches for achieving lossless inference using both MAD-based and LUT-based methods.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Design &amp; Implementation: TL</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since table lookups require SIMD instructions operating on 8-bit data, a potential conflict arises when enumerating sums that might overflow if stored in 8-bit integers. T-MAC addresses this issue by quantizing the accumulated sum to int8; however, this approach introduces additional losses, preventing lossless inference. To resolve this, we introduce the pack-and-unpack technique. First, we maintain the sums as int16 without additional quantization and split the int16 enumerated sums into two parts using the pack instruction. Then, during the indexing process, we apply the table lookup twice. Afterward, we use the unpack instruction to concatenate the two parts, ultimately obtaining the desired int16 result. Kernels that utilize typical additional quantization are TL1_0 and TL2_0, whereas those that use the pack-and-unpack technique are TL1_1 and TL2_1.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2 </span>Design &amp; Implementation: I2_S</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to inconsistency with training schemes, existing element-wise MAD-based methods do not enable lossless inference for BitNet b1.58. In Bitnet.cpp, I2_S is designed based on the element-wise approach, adhering strictly to the ternary weight and per-tensor int8 activation quantization settings of BitNet b1.58 training, thereby ensuring lossless inference. Furthermore, I2_S performs comparably with TQ2_0 and supports mpGEMM dimensions <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> that are multiples of 128, while TQ2_0 only supports multiples of 256. As a result, we have optimized the MAD-based solutions and integrated the implementation into Bitnet.cpp.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated the performance of Bitnet.cpp for end-to-end edge inference for ternary LLM. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, Bitnet.cpp significantly improves ternary LLM edge inference performance across different CPU architectures and model sizes under the sub-2-bits-per-weight condition. For quality evaluation, compared to Float16, TL1_0 and TL2_0 exhibit negligible loss, whereas I2_S, TL1_1, and TL2_1 achieve lossless in BitNet b1.58.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Speed Evaluation</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1 </span>Devices</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted a performance evaluation of Bitnet.cpp on two devices: the Apple M2 Ultra and the Intel i7-13700H. These devices represent the ARM and x86 architectures, respectively, covering most edge devices and ensuring broad applicability and reliable performance results for Bitnet.cpp.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.2 </span>Baselines</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted experiments from two perspectives: lossless inference and fast inference. For the lossless inference aspect, we chose llama.cpp Float16 as the baseline and compared it with I2_S from Bitnet.cpp. This comparison evaluates the lossless inference performance of Bitnet.cpp, demonstrating its improvements in both accuracy and speed. For the fast inference aspect, we conducted experiments based on the two features of TL2_0: element-wise and LUT-based. llama.cpp includes two element-wise MAD-based solutions, TQ1_0 and TQ2_0. To neutralize the effect of bpw, TQ1_0, which has a bpw nearly identical to TL2_0, was selected for comparison. This comparison aims to evaluate the performance differences between MAD-based and LUT-based solutions. For T-MAC, a bit-wise LUT-based solution, the 2-bit kernel was selected for comparison with TL2_0 to assess performance differences between element-wise and bit-wise methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.3 </span>End-to-end Inference Speed</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated the token generation speed of Bitnet.cpp and observed a significant speed advantage across different CPU architectures and model sizes compared to baselines. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 3.1.2 Implementation: TL ‣ 3.1 Fast Edge Inference ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, I2_S achieves up to a 6.25x speedup compared to Float16, demonstrating that Bitnet.cpp provides a comprehensive advantage in both accuracy and speed. Furthermore, TL2_0 outperforms T-MAC by up to 2.32x on the Intel i7-13700H and by up to 1.19x on the Apple M2 Ultra, indicating a notable improvement in LUT-based mpGEMM performance. Moreover, TL2_0 surpasses TQ1_0, with up to 1.33x speedup on the Intel i7-13700H and 1.65x on the Apple M2 Ultra, further improving performance in element-wise mpGEMM with bpw below 2. As detailed in Table <a href="#A5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix E Performance ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, TL2_0 reaches 7.45 tokens/s on the Apple M2 Ultra and 1.69 tokens/s on the Intel i7-13700H, outperforming previous ternary kernels in 100B ternary LLM inference on edge devices. These findings highlight the significant inference benefits of Bitnet.cpp.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Quality Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We used the bitnet_b1_58-large<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://huggingface.co/1bitLLM/bitnet_b1_58-large" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/1bitLLM/bitnet_b1_58-large</a></span></span></span> model and the perplexity<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/tree/master/examples/perplexity" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/tree/master/examples/perplexity</a></span></span></span> tool from llama.cpp for quality evaluation. For baselines, Float16 and Q4_0 from llama.cpp were selected for comparison with Bitnet.cpp. For tasks, we used WikiText2<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merity et al. (2016)</a></cite> to measure perplexity (the lower, the better), HellaSwag<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zellers et al. (2019)</a></cite> and WinoGrande<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sakaguchi et al. (2021)</a></cite> to measure accuracy (the higher, the better). As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Quality Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, both TL1_0 and TL2_0 achieve nearly identical perplexity compared to Float16 on WikiText2 and maintain accuracy comparable to Float16 on WinoGrande and HellaSwag. I2_S, TL1_1, and TL2_1 exhibit lossless performance relative to Float16 across all tasks. These results indicate that the loss introduced by Bitnet.cpp is negligible.</p>
</div>

</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.2.8.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2pt;padding-bottom:2pt;">

<span id="S4.T2.2.8.4.1.1" class="ltx_p">43.0</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T2.2.9" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.2.9.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2pt;padding-bottom:2pt;">
<span id="S4.T2.2.9.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:28.5pt;">
<span id="S4.T2.2.9.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">I2_S</span>
</span></td>

<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LUT-based mpGEMM</span>
Previous research has explored the application of LUT-based mpGEMM in deep learning. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ganji et al. (2023)</a></cite> employs LUT-based mpGEMM to accelerate computations in convolutional neural networks, while <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davis Blalock (2021)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al. (2023)</a></cite> utilize this approach to process vector-quantized activations. For LLM inference, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maleki (2023)</a></cite> apply LUT-based GEMM on GPUs. However, in practice, these methods are often slower than MAD-based approaches, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">cut ()</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">bit ()</a></cite>, due to the inefficiency of rapid table access on GPU.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM Inference</span>
FlashAttention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao, 2023</a>)</cite> introduces an innovative approach to GPU attention kernel design. VLLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and TensorRT-LLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">trt, </a>)</cite> have optimized end-to-end inference performance using systematic techniques. Powerinfer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xue et al. (2024)</a></cite> proposes novel strategies that intelligently balance workloads across heterogeneous devices, improving overall inference efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM Quantization</span>
Post-training quantization (PTQ) refers to converting a full-precision LLM to a low-precision without retraining, with related works including <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chee et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frantar et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al. (2024)</a></cite>. However, PTQ inevitably results in quantization loss. In contrast, Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) effectively avoids this issue. QAT involves retraining a pretrained model to obtain a quantized model, thus mitigating quantization loss. Relevant works include <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al. (2024)</a></cite>. BitNet B1.58 adopts QAT, creating conditions for lossless inference in the system.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, by optimizing mpGEMM, we address the inefficiencies caused by the conflicts of non-integer bpw in ternary LLMs with memory access alignment rules, and enable lossless inference for BitNet b1.58. Our key idea is to utilize a finer-grained element-wise scheme instead of bit-wise, and consistent with BitNet b1.58 training schemes. Based on our key ideas, we develop Bitnet.cpp, featuring TL, the first element-wise LUT-based mpGEMM kernel for ternary LLMs, and I2_S, the first lossless MAD-based kernel for BitNet b1.58. The practical outcomes of our research are noteworthy. We have demonstrated that Bitnet.cpp achieves up to 6.25x speedup compared to baselines and provided lossless inference for BitNet b1.58. To enhance the generality of our research, we extended the TL to ELUT for low-bit LLMs, highlighting its efficiency and potential. This paper presents extensive work on optimizing edge inference for ternary LLMs from both algorithmic and engineering perspectives. It offers the research community new insights into handling ternary and non-integer bpw weights, shows the practical advantages of ternary LLMs and presents the industry with innovative solutions for deploying fast, lossless LLMs on edge devices.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Bitnet.cpp has the following limitations:</p>
<ul id="Sx1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="Sx1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="Sx1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Bitnet.cpp currently only provides a practical solution for ternary LLM inference on edge devices. In the future, we plan to extend the Bitnet.cpp to offer efficient inference solutions for ternary LLMs across multiple devices.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="Sx1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="Sx1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Bitnet.cpp is specifically designed for ternary LLMs, with a relatively narrow range of applicable model architectures. In response to this, we have expanded the element-wise LUT-based (ELUT) method to cover low-bit ranges in the appendix. However, it still lacks support from actual LLMs other than ternary ones.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="Sx1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="Sx1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Bitnet.cpp does not discuss in detail the acceleration specifics of LLMs during the prefilling stage, as there has been a shift in the resource bottleneck from being memory-bound during the decoding stage to computation-bound during the prefilling stage. Therefore, the original optimization methods are no longer applicable, and we will continue to explore optimization methods for the prefilling stage.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the appendix, we extend the concept of element-wise LUT-based solutions beyond ternary LLMs, analyzing its capabilities and potential from a more general perspective.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Insight</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we will analyze the computational complexity and memory access complexity of the element-wise LUT-based (ELUT) mpGEMM algorithm. Based on this analysis, we will compare our results with those of MAD-based solutions and bit-wise LUT-based solutions, drawing the conclusion that the ELUT algorithm exhibits comprehensive advantages in both computation and memory access compared to previous algorithms.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Complexity</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In general, mpGEMM requires two steps to complete: the preprocessing stage and the accumulation stage. As shown in Algorithm <a href="#algorithm1" title="In A.1 Complexity ‣ Appendix A Insight ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, for the MAD-based solution, the preprocessing stage involves quantizing the floating-point activations to integers, with a computational complexity of <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(NK)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(NK)</annotation></semantics></math> and a memory access complexity of <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(NK)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(NK)</annotation></semantics></math>. In the accumulation stage, the MAD-based solution performs element-wise multiplication and accumulation for the K corresponding elements across M rows and N columns, resulting in a computational complexity of <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(MNK)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(MNK)</annotation></semantics></math> and a memory access complexity of <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(MNK)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(MNK)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Algorithm <a href="#algorithm2" title="In A.1 Complexity ‣ Appendix A Insight ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, for ELUT, the preprocessing stage involves first performing quantization to quantize the floating-point activations into <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="NK/g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">NK/g</annotation></semantics></math> groups, and then enumerating the <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{g}</annotation></semantics></math> possible values within each group to construct the Lookup Table. The computational complexity of this process is <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(NKC^{g}/g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(NKC^{g}/g)</annotation></semantics></math>, and the memory access complexity is also <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(NKC^{g}/g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(NKC^{g}/g)</annotation></semantics></math>. In the accumulation stage, ELUT performs lookup and accumulation operations group by group. The computational complexity of this process is <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(MNK/g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(MNK/g)</annotation></semantics></math>, while the memory access complexity is <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(MNKC^{g}/g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(MNKC^{g}/g)</annotation></semantics></math> because the entire Lookup Table must be loaded for each group.</p>
</div>
<figure id="algorithm1" class="ltx_float ltx_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="algorithm1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span>MAD-based mpGEMM</figcaption>

<span id="algorithm1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text"><span id="algorithm1.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span> </span>Activation <math id="algorithm1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> of shape <math id="algorithm1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N,K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N,K</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.2" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.2.1" class="ltx_text"><span id="algorithm1.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span> </span>Weights <math id="algorithm1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> of shape <math id="algorithm1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M,K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M,K</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="algorithm1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\in\mathbb{Z},\ |W|=C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℤ</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\in\mathbb{Z},\ |W|=C</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.3" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.3.1" class="ltx_text"><span id="algorithm1.4.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output:</span> </span>Result matrix <math id="algorithm1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> of shape <math id="algorithm1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M,N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M,N</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
