</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.5" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/* </span><span id="algorithm1.4.5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M-complexity <math id="algorithm1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> Memory Access Complexity  */</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.6" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/* </span><span id="algorithm1.4.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Phase1 : Preprocessing  */</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.7" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/* </span><span id="algorithm1.4.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C-complexity : <math id="algorithm1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(NK)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(NK)</annotation></semantics></math> / M-complexity : <math id="algorithm1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(NK)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(NK)</annotation></semantics></math>  */</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.8" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1</span></span>
            <math id="algorithm1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{q}=\text{Quantization}(A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Quantization</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{q}=\text{Quantization}(A)</annotation></semantics></math> 
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.9" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/* </span><span id="algorithm1.4.9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Phase2 : Accumulation  */</span>
</div>

            <span id="algorithm1.4.11.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <em id="algorithm1.4.11.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="algorithm1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m,n\leftarrow 1\text{ to }M,N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic"> to </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m,n\leftarrow 1\text{ to }M,N</annotation></semantics></math></em> <span id="algorithm1.4.11.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>

              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3</span></span>
            <math id="algorithm1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R[n,m]=\sum_{k=1}^{K}(A_{q}[n,k]*W[m,k])" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R[n,m]=\sum_{k=1}^{K}(A_{q}[n,k]*W[m,k])</annotation></semantics></math>

              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm2.4.14.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4</span></span>

</div>
<div id="algorithm2.4.18" class="ltx_listingline">
</div>
</div>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Through theoretical analysis, we can identify several interesting insights. First, ELUT has an advantage over the MAD-based solution in terms of computational complexity for LLM inference. The overall computational complexity of the MAD-based solution is <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(MNK)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(MNK)</annotation></semantics></math>, while ELUT is <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="max(O(NKC^{g}/g),O(MNK/g))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">max(O(NKC^{g}/g),O(MNK/g))</annotation></semantics></math>. This implies that as long as <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{g}&lt;M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{g}&lt;M</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, ELUT requires fewer computations for mpGEMM. In LLMs, the value of <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., the hidden size, is generally large. In contrast, the <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> value for ternary LLMs is only 3 and <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is only 2 or 3. Therefore, ELUT is computationally more efficient than the MAD-based solution.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">However, ELUT has a disadvantage in terms of memory access complexity compared to the MAD-based solution. The memory access complexity of the MAD-based solution is <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(MNK)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(MNK)</annotation></semantics></math>, while the LUT-based solution has a memory access complexity of <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(MNKC^{g}/g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(MNKC^{g}/g)</annotation></semantics></math>. In practical implementations, we employ optimization techniques such as element-wise mirror consolidation and LUT-centric data layout to reduce memory access complexity, thereby significantly mitigating the overhead caused by memory access.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/analysis_plot.svg" id="A1.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/173;" width="476" height="173"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Multi-threaded end-to-end inference performance of the 3.8B model on Intel i7 13700H.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Compared to MAD-based: More Practical</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In fact, when deploying LLMs on current edge devices, we often face the limitation of using only a very small number of threads. Under such circumstances, the constraints on computational resources are maximized, making computational complexity a critical factor. In contrast, due to the limited number of threads, memory access is unlikely to reach bandwidth limits. In this context, ELUT, with its computational complexity being only <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>g</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{g}</annotation></semantics></math> of that of the MAD-based solution in most cases, is expected to outperform the MAD-based solution in real-world inference scenarios for LLMs. Therefore, ELUT is more suitable for deployment in practical scenarios than the MAD-based solution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Compared to Bit-Wise : More Fine-grained</h3>

<figure id="A1.T3" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A1.T3.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>A comparison table of bpw from bit-wise and element-wise for different weight cardinality. <math id="A1.T3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> represents the weight cardinality, <math id="A1.T3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> indicates to group size, <math id="A1.T3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bpw_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bpw_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes bit-wise bpw, <math id="A1.T3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bpw_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bpw_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> refers to element-wise bpw.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although we have demonstrated that ELUT outperforms MAD-based solutions in terms of performance with low thread counts, the bit-wise LUT-based solution also exhibits this advantage. The advantage of the ELUT method over the bit-wise method lies in its finer granularity of LUTs, shifting from bit-based to element-based, ensuring a more information-preserving compression of weights.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Returning to the computational complexity, in most cases, the computational complexity of the LUT method is <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(MNK/g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(MNK/g)</annotation></semantics></math>. For ternary LLMs, when <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=3</annotation></semantics></math>, the complexity is reduced by a factor of <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{6}</annotation></semantics></math> compared to <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=2</annotation></semantics></math>. In terms of memory access complexity, since mirror consolidation is used when <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=3</annotation></semantics></math>, we can compute the memory access complexity for <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=3</annotation></semantics></math> as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A1.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\frac{MNK3^{2}}{2})=O(\frac{MNK3^{3}/2}{3})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\frac{MNK3^{2}}{2})=O(\frac{MNK3^{3}/2}{3})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Based on this, since the <math id="A1.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bpw" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bpw</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="A1.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=3</annotation></semantics></math> is approximately 1/6 lower than when <math id="A1.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=2</annotation></semantics></math> and memory access complexity is similar, we observe that when using the ELUT method on ternary LLMs inference, both computation and memory access are reduced compared to the bit-wise method. Similarly, as Table <a href="#A1.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ A.3 Compared to Bit-Wise : More Fine-grained ‣ Appendix A Insight ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shown, the same conclusion can be extended to the case where <math id="A1.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C\neq 2^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>≠</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C\neq 2^{n}</annotation></semantics></math>. This provides theoretical guidance for TL implementation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Analysis</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Memory-Computation Trade-off Decoding</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During the execution of a kernel, the execution speed is determined by both instruction computation speed and data access speed. The instruction computation speed is related to the computational complexity, instruction types, and the depth of the pipeline, while the data access speed depends on the memory access complexity, locality, and the type of memory being accessed. The kernel execution speed is ultimately determined by the smaller of these two values. Naturally, we refer to computation-related consumptions as <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">computation</span> consumptions and data-access-related consumptions as <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">memory</span> consumptions. Thus, optimizing kernel performance is essentially a process of exploring the compute-memory trade-off. In fact, ELUT outperforms previous approaches in achieving a better trade-off, resulting in performance improvements. This can be clearly observed from both the compute and memory perspectives by analyzing performance gap for TQ1_0 and T-MAC with TL2_0.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Towards Memory: Compared to T-MAC</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the previous section, we provided a detailed theoretical analysis of the LUT-based solution, showing that the memory access complexity of ELUT and T-MAC is equivalent, but with a lower bpw, resulting in reduced memory access requirements. In the following, we validate this conclusion with practical examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In fact, TL2_0 has an advantage over T-MAC in terms of bpw, which enhances the performance ceiling of memory-intensive LUT-based solutions to some extent. As a result, significant performance improvements are observed, particularly in low bandwidth environments. As shown in Figure <a href="#A1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A.1 Complexity ‣ Appendix A Insight ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> (b), TL2_0 achieves a performance improvement over T-MAC in a multi-threaded environment. Notably, the performance of TL2_0 continues to improve as the number of threads reaches 5, while the speed of T-MAC begins to decline. This indicates that TL2_0 reaches the memory-bound state later than T-MAC, thereby raising the performance ceiling.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Towards Compute: Compared to TQ1_0</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the previous section, we theoretically verified that ELUT exhibits lower computational complexity compared to the MAD-based solution. To ensure a fair comparison, we selected TQ1_0, which has a bpw almost identical to that of TL2_0, for the comparative experiment. The results show that LUT-based solutions offer an advantage over MAD-based solutions in terms of computation-related consumption, leading to a significant performance improvement. As shown in Figure <a href="#A1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A.1 Complexity ‣ Appendix A Insight ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> (a), the shape of performance curves of TL2_0 and TQ1_0 in a multi-threaded environment are nearly identical, with TL2_0 consistently outperforming TQ1_0 across all threads. This further supports our conclusion that LUT-based solutions have an advantage over MAD-based solutions in computation-related consumption, resulting in a significant performance increase.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F10" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A2.F10.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:155.3pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/potential.svg" id="A2.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:215/161;" width="215" height="161"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>ELUT performance potential curve.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A2.F10.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:155.3pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/twin.svg" id="A2.F10.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:215/161;" width="215" height="161"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Throughput and Bandwidth curve, tested with bitnet-b1.58-large on intel core i5-13400F.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Potential</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After evaluating the performance of ELUT, we have observed that it has a comprehensive advantage over other methods. However, we believe that ELUT has not yet reached its theoretical performance limit. In the following, we will analyze the hardware limitations affecting ELUT and estimate its theoretical performance in the absence of such constraints. This analysis aims to explore the potential of ELUT and provide insights for future hardware designs targeting low-bit LLMs inference.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Bandwidth</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Bandwidth is the data transfer rate between memory and the processor, and it also determines the execution rate of kernels. Considering that ELUT has a higher memory access complexity than the MAD-based solution, bandwidth has a significant influence on overall end-to-end inference speed. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 3.1.2 Implementation: TL ‣ 3.1 Fast Edge Inference ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, it is evident that TL2_0 demonstrates a more pronounced acceleration effect on T-MAC for Intel i7-13700H compared to Apple M2 Ultra. The main reason for this phenomenon lies in the significant difference in maximum bandwidth between the two edge devices. In fact, the Apple M2 Ultra has a maximum bandwidth exceeding 800 GB/s, while the maximum bandwidth of the Intel i7-13700H is less than 100 GB/s. As shown in Figure <a href="#A2.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ B.3 Towards Compute: Compared to TQ1_0 ‣ Appendix B Analysis ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we used PCM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">PCM ()</a></cite> tool to measure the token throughput and bandwidth at different thread counts and compared them side by side. It is clear that the shape of token throughput and bandwidth curves are nearly identical. When the thread count reaches 4, the token throughput also reaches its maximum value due to the saturation of the bandwidth, causing the end-to-end inference speed to reach its peak. Therefore, we can conclude that the maximum bandwidth limits the potential of ELUT. Building on this, as shown in Figure <a href="#A2.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ B.3 Towards Compute: Compared to TQ1_0 ‣ Appendix B Analysis ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we estimated the end-to-end inference speed when the bandwidth is increased. We anticipate that, with the increase in maximum bandwidth, ELUT will reach the memory-bound state later, resulting in a higher end-to-end inference speed, with the upper bound still determined by the theoretical maximum bandwidth. This estimation validates our theoretical analysis of ELUT. Moreover, we are pleased to note that there is currently a trend towards increasing the bandwidth of edge devices, which will further unlock the potential of ELUT.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T4" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A3.T4.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A3.T4.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A3.T4.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">Instruction Set</td>
<td id="A3.T4.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">LUT-based</td>
<td id="A3.T4.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">MAD-based</td>
<td id="A3.T4.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_border_t"></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T4.2.2" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A3.T4.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">_mm256_shuffle_epi8</td>
<td id="A3.T4.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">_mm256_maddubs_epi16</td>

<td id="A3.T4.2.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_border_b"></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Core instructions in AVX2 and Neon for LUT-based and MAD-based mpGEMM.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Instructions Throughput</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SIMD instructions are commonly used to implement kernels on CPUs, as SIMD allows a single instruction to process multiple data elements simultaneously, achieving computation parallelism and acceleration.
For SIMD instructions, two metrics determine the performance of the instruction: instruction throughput, which determines the number of instructions that can be completed in a single clock, and instruction latency, which determines the number of clocks required to complete a single instruction. On modern CPUs, since MAD operations are widely used, common architectures such as x86 and ARM have made specific optimizations to ensure high instruction throughput for these operations (as shown in Table <a href="#A3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ C.1 Bandwidth ‣ Appendix C Potential ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). For example, in the x86 architecture with AVX2 instructions, a single MAD instruction can complete an int8 multiply-accumulate operation and convert the result to int16. However, for ELUT, we need to use three types of instructions—TBL (table lookup), ADD (accumulation), and CVT (type conversion)—to accomplish the same task. Although the AVX documentation <span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html</a></span></span></span> states that the latency of the MAD instruction is 5 cycles, which is greater than the latency of the TBL instruction, both instructions have the same throughput. This implies that, under reasonable pipeline scheduling, the theoretical completion time for MAD and TBL instructions is the same. We validated this on an Intel i5-13400F, where the completion time for a single MAD instruction was <span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3.77 ns</span>, and for a single TBL instruction, it was <span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3.70 ns</span>, which is nearly identical. However, since the table lookup must be followed by addition and conversion (TBL+ADD+CVT), this sequence inevitably leads to a reduction in throughput. We observed that completing the same task with TBL+ADD+CVT took <span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6.20 ns</span>, approximately 68% longer than the raw latency of a single MAD instruction. This highlights that, in terms of throughput, the table lookup followed by the accumulation method suffers significant performance loss due to insufficient hardware support.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In previous work, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mo et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al. (2024)</a></cite> was implemented in hardware on GPUs and FPGAs, respectively, as solutions similar to ELUT, and they achieved performance improvements over MAD-based solutions. This suggests that providing better hardware support for ELUT on edge devices is highly promising. As shown in Figure <a href="#A2.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ B.3 Towards Compute: Compared to TQ1_0 ‣ Appendix B Analysis ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we estimated the performance of ELUT with hardware support, and the results indicate a significant performance boost when bandwidth is not a bottleneck. We sincerely hope that the exploration of ELUT’s potential can inspire future hardware designs to fully unlock ELUT’s capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Register Length</h3>

<figure id="A3.F11" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.11880v1/latency.svg" id="A3.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/357;" width="476" height="357"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span> Register length and raw latency relationship graph.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The length of registers also imposes a limitation on the performance of ELUT. Taking AVX2 as an example, the lookup width of the TBL SIMD instruction is 128 bits, which means that it can look up 16 int8 values in one operation. Clearly, from an element-wise perspective, all the possible values of <math id="A3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{g}</annotation></semantics></math> that we enumerate need to be covered in a single lookup. Otherwise, we would need to use a bit-wise approach, performing bit-by-bit lookups, which sacrifices the memory access benefits obtained from the element-wise method. For example, in the case of ternary LLMs, with the limitation of 128-bit register length, we can enumerate at most <math id="A3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{3^{3}}{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mn>2</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{3^{3}}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> possible values in the lookup table, which restricts <math id="A3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g\leq 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g\leq 3</annotation></semantics></math>. Assuming we disregard the limitation of instruction length, we simulate a longer instruction length using the original instructions without considering precision. As shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ C.3 Register Length ‣ Appendix C Potential ‣ Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, as the length of SIMD registers increases, the number of enumerable <math id="A3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> values grows, thereby significantly reducing computational complexity. Theoretically, when <math id="A3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{g}=M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{g}=M</annotation></semantics></math>, the computational complexity introduced by enumerating LUTs surpasses that of table lookup and accumulation, and further increasing the length of SIMD registers no longer yields additional benefits. It is significant that the <math id="A3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> values we can currently enumerate are still far from the intersection point. Therefore, increasing the register length provides a definite benefit in terms of computational complexity. This also indicates that the potential of ELUT has not yet reached its theoretical limit.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>

          <math id="algorithm3.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="IndexWeight[m,k]=Pack(W[m,2k],W[m,2k+1])" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">IndexWeight[m,k]=Pack(W[m,2k],W[m,2k+1])</annotation></semantics></math>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>TL2 Kernel compresses every three full-precision weights into a 1-bit sign (<span id="A4.T6.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">0</span> or <span id="A4.T6.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">1</span>) and a 4-bit index. </figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="algorithm4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 4</span> </span>TL2 mpGEMM</figcaption>
<div id="algorithm4.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_lst_numbers_left ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="algorithm4.4.1" class="ltx_listingline">
<span id="algorithm4.4.1.1" class="ltx_text"><span id="algorithm4.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span> </span>Activation <math id="algorithm4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> of shape <math id="algorithm4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N,K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N,K</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm4.4.2" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm4.4.2.1" class="ltx_text"><span id="algorithm4.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span> </span>Weights <math id="algorithm4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> of shape <math id="algorithm4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M,K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M,K</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>

</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Comparison of inference speed across different CPU (Unit: Tokens/Second) in an unlimited thread setting. <math id="A5.T7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(x)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the bits per weight, where <math id="A5.T7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> denotes specific value. "N/A" indicates that the tested CPU cannot host the specified model size with the given kernel. The token generation speed was determined by calculating the average results from 10 tests conducted across different devices using diverse methodologies.</figcaption>

        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
